items.title: UK Workplace AI Literacy Checklist
items.summary: A practical checklist for managers introducing AI at work, with role-specific literacy, data handling, output checking and escalation controls.
sections: Know what is being used
List the AI tools staff are allowed to use.
Record the business tasks each tool supports.
Identify which teams, contractors and service providers use them.
Teach the failure modes
Explain hallucination, uncertainty and misleading confidence.
Show staff what information must be checked against an authoritative source.
Use examples from the organisation’s real tasks rather than generic demos.
Set data boundaries
Define what personal, confidential or client data may enter each tool.
Document retention, training and supplier data-use terms.
Give staff a safe route when they are unsure whether data can be used.
Make human oversight real
Name the decisions that require human approval.
Ensure reviewers have time and authority to challenge outputs.
Record incidents and feed lessons back into guidance.

items.title: Deepfake Verification Checklist
items.summary: A step-by-step verification checklist for suspicious video, audio and images, designed to reduce reliance on visual guessing or a single detector score.
sections: Preserve the evidence
Save the original URL and publication context.
Keep the original file where law and policy allow.
Note when and where the item was first encountered.
Check provenance
Find the earliest credible source rather than the loudest repost.
Look for trustworthy provenance metadata or platform disclosure.
Compare with official channels for the person or organisation depicted.
Corroborate independently
Use reverse image or frame search where useful.
Look for independent reporting of the same event or claim.
Treat automated detector scores as supporting evidence, not a final verdict.
Escalate high-stakes cases
Pause payments, publication or disciplinary action while verification is unresolved.
Use specialist forensic support when consequences are serious.
Document what was checked and what remains uncertain.

items.title: AI Procurement Questions for Small Businesses
items.summary: Questions for buying AI tools without discovering the real data, security and lock-in terms after the trial has already spread through the business.
sections: Purpose and evidence
What exact task does the tool improve?
What evidence shows the benefit for a business like ours?
What manual or conventional software option are we comparing it with?
Data and privacy
What data leaves our systems?
Is our content used to train or improve models?
Where is data stored and how can it be deleted or exported?
Security and control
Which models and subcontractors sit underneath the service?
How are permissions and administrator actions controlled?
How are security incidents and material product changes communicated?
Commercial reality
What happens to price after the trial?
Can we leave without losing our data or workflow history?
Who owns generated output and who carries responsibility for errors?

items.title: Responsible AI Checklist for Managers
items.summary: A practical manager checklist for ownership, data, human review, monitoring and incident handling around AI systems.
sections: Name the owner
Assign a named owner for each material AI use.
Record purpose, affected users and the decision it influences.
Set a date for review rather than approving a tool forever.
Bound the system
Specify approved data sources and prohibited inputs.
Limit permissions to what the task requires.
Define which outputs are advice and which can trigger action.
Check people and impact
Identify who may be disadvantaged by errors or bias.
Give users a way to challenge consequential outcomes.
Make human review meaningful rather than ceremonial.
Monitor and stop
Track failures and complaints as well as success metrics.
Reassess after supplier or model changes.
Keep a practical kill switch or fallback process for material failures.

items.title: AI Agent Risk Checklist
items.summary: A pre-deployment checklist for AI agents that can call tools or take actions, focused on permissions, observability, reversibility and escalation.
sections: Define the job
Write the goal and stopping condition in plain language.
List the tools and data the agent genuinely needs.
Prefer deterministic automation where the task is already deterministic.
Restrict authority
Apply least-privilege permissions.
Require confirmation for irreversible, financial or external actions.
Separate test and production credentials.
Observe behaviour
Log tool calls, actions and important intermediate decisions.
Test malformed inputs, unavailable tools and conflicting instructions.
Measure failure recovery, not just successful demo runs.
Plan recovery
Make actions reversible where practical.
Define a human escalation route and kill switch.
Re-test after model, prompt, tool or permission changes.

items.title: AI in Regulated Industries Evidence Map
items.summary: A compact map of primary sources for healthcare, finance, data protection, security and AI literacy, with questions to ask before relying on a vendor claim.
sections: Healthcare
Check regulator status for the exact product and intended use.
Separate device authorisation from evidence of benefit in your setting.
Review monitoring, workflow and human-oversight evidence.
Financial services
Check FCA and Bank of England material for sector-specific expectations and adoption evidence.
Map third-party model and cloud dependencies.
Distinguish assisted decisions from full autonomy.
Data protection and security
Map personal-data purpose, lawful basis, minimisation and rights.
Use security guidance across development, deployment and operation.
Treat supplier changes as a trigger for review.
Governance evidence
Keep source dates and links beside important claims.
Record limitations as well as benefits.
Prefer regulator, government, standards and peer-reviewed sources over vendor summaries.

items.title: EU AI Act Article 50 Readiness Checklist
items.summary: A practical pre-2-August checklist for mapping AI transparency duties, notices, marking, ownership and evidence without pretending every AI use has the same obligation.
sections: Map the systems and roles
List interactive AI and generative systems that reach users or the public.
Record whether the organisation is acting as provider, deployer or both for each use.
Identify the EU market, users and content flows that could bring a use into scope.
Check the transparency trigger
Identify where people interact directly with an AI system.
Identify generated or manipulated image, audio, video and text that is published or shown externally.
Flag deepfakes, emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation uses for specific review.
Design the notice or marking
Make notices visible at the point where they are useful rather than burying them in general terms.
For provider-side generated-content marking, document how machine-readable marking is produced and tested where required.
For deployer disclosures, define the wording, placement and exceptions that apply to the actual use case.
Assign ownership and evidence
Name the person or role responsible for each transparency control.
Keep records of scope decisions, system versions, notices, labelling and tests.
Create an escalation route for uncertain cases and for systems whose behaviour or use changes.
Recheck after launch
Test whether users can actually see and understand the disclosure.
Monitor vendor and model changes that could alter provider/deployer responsibilities.
Review the implementation against current Commission guidance and any sector-specific obligations.
